case.cot: This respondent sees personal effort as central to getting ahead: she rates hard work as very important and her own good education as very important, and she holds that how hard a person works at the job should be essential in deciding pay. Ambition is the motivational side of those same qualities — the drive that pushes someone to work hard and invest in education — so it belongs in the same high tier. Her pattern of reserving 'essential' for outside advantages like coming from a wealthy family or knowing the right people, while placing effort-based traits at 'very important,' fits rating ambition, an internal drive rather than an external leg-up, as very important. case.question: How important are opportunities for advancement to you personally?
case.questionZh: 对你个人来说，工作中有晋升机会有多重要？
case.cot: Work carries clear instrumental weight for this respondent: he rates high income as important, would rather work longer hours for more money, strongly rejects the idea of staying with his firm when another job pays quite a bit more, and considers it likely he will look for a new employer within the year. That pattern of active, earnings-oriented career engagement makes opportunities for advancement a natural priority, since promotion is the usual route to the better pay and position he is evidently open to. At the same time, his 'very important' ratings are reserved for the intrinsic side of work — an interesting job, independence, social usefulness, and personal contact — while income itself is only 'important,' so advancement plausibly lands at the same level: a genuinely important concern, but not his single top one. Therefore, the answer is 2.
case.cotZh: 这位受访者很看重工作带来的实际回报。他认为高收入“重要”，愿意延长工时来多挣钱，非常不同意“即使另一份工作薪水高很多，也要留在现单位”的说法，也觉得自己未来一年可能会另找雇主。从这种主动争取更好收入的态度看，他自然会重视晋升机会，因为晋升通常能带来更高的薪酬和更好的职位。另一方面，他把“非常重要”留给了工作本身的特点，例如工作有趣、能独立工作、对社会有用、能与人接触。高收入只被他评为“重要”，因此，把晋升机会也放在这一档符合他的回答：他确实在意晋升，但没有把它列为头等大事。因此选 2。

case.cot: This respondent sees getting ahead as primarily earned — hard work is essential and a good education very important — while dismissing fixed advantages like coming from a wealthy family and rating bribes as not very important. Yet they also consider political connections fairly important, which places relational ties in a middle category: a real lever that complements effort and credentials rather than replacing them. Knowing the right people belongs to that same relational category, distinct from inherited status or payoffs, so a moderately high rating fits their pattern. Their view of society as a pyramid with strong rich–poor conflict, together with a general wariness toward other people, plausibly reinforces the sense that who you know shapes access to opportunity, even if less decisively than merit.
